q6.answer: Each upload change carries a client-generated change_id (UUID). In one server transaction the server first looks it up in the applied-changes table. If found, it returns the stored outcome (accepted, or conflict plus the conflict note id) and applies nothing. If new, it applies the change and stores the outcome under that change_id in the same transaction as the write and log entry.

q7.answer: In a cursor stored in the phone's local SQLite database, holding the last log seq applied. It is updated only in the same local transaction that applies a downloaded page, set to that page's next_cursor.

q8.answer: A partial response applies nothing and the cursor has not moved, since it advances only in the same transaction that applies a page. The next sync refetches from the unchanged cursor, so nothing is skipped or applied twice (upserts ignore versions at or below the local one).

q9.answer: The upload response returns a conflict outcome for that change_id with the conflict note id. The phone removes the outbox row and resets the displayed note to its last known server copy. The user's text is not lost because it is in the conflict note, which arrives on the next download like any other log entry.

q10.answer: Only after the server's ack for it (accepted or conflict result). A lost response, failed request or app kill leaves the row in place and it is retried with the same change_id.

q11.answer: The phone updates only its stored server copy (server_version, server_title, server_body) and leaves the displayed draft alone. The queued change keeps its old base version, so it will conflict when uploaded, which is intended. The loser is saved as a conflict note.

q12.answer: The edit is saved locally right away and becomes a separate pending outbox row, because the in-flight row is not overwritten. When the ack arrives, the new row's base version is filled in from the acked version, or from the conflict outcome if the upload lost. I did not fully work out what happens in the conflict case beyond that, or how the new row gets a change_id and avoids two changes for one note in a batch.
